Anthropic Lives Up to Wall Street Hype, but AI Doubts Linger
 
Plus, Kushner floats a Ukraine peace deal that would upend U.S. policy, and the snack sailors aboard the USS George Washington can’t get enough of
 
 
BRENDAN MCDERMID/REUTERS
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Wall Street was looking to Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO for an answer to a big question: Are investors still willing to bet on the AI boom? The answer wasn’t quite so simple.

 

The company behind Claude raised $81 billion in the largest IPO ever. Its shares opened more than 30% above the offering price Thursday but closed up 17%, while the broader market slumped. Our reporters explain why Anthropic’s debut was a success for the company and its backers, yet failed to revive the AI trade.

 

But there may be reason to distinguish Anthropic’s prospects from those of the AI industry as a whole. Asa Fitch argues that a potentially more lucrative phase of the artificial-intelligence boom is taking shape, one in which companies like Anthropic could draw more profits from applying the technology rather than building its infrastructure.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• President Trump’s whirlwind trip to Asia offered a glimpse into how he hopes to cement his legacy through foreign-policy breakthroughs.

 

• White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving his role, a departure that comes as the Trump administration responds to a wave of cyber threats.

 

• The head of Israel’s Mossad spy agency pushed for renewed U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran during a visit to the U.S. last week.

 

• The Fed approved smaller pay raises for employees at its 12 regional banks, with minimum annual increases falling to 1% next year from 3% this year.

 

• Our tax columnist took the pulse of Bogleheads at the annual gathering of the Vanguard founder’s disciples. She loves a good tax discussion, and this crowd didn’t disappoint. Here is what she learned.

• China’s tech champions were already limping as they tried to keep pace with U.S. competitors at the cutting edge of AI. New U.S. rules issued in the aftermath of the scandal at Nvidia are set to slow them down even more.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Parents are flying blind in a booming autism-therapy industry.

 

Applied behavior analysis has become the most widely used form of autism treatment, often recommended by doctors and covered by insurance. But a boom in treatment has attracted thousands of providers, ranging from autism-therapy experts to business people with little healthcare experience and, in some cases, outright fraudsters. With little oversight and wide variations in quality, parents are struggling to figure out what might truly help their children. Dan Frosch examines the challenges families face in navigating the industry.

 

5.

 

Kushner floats a Ukraine peace deal that would upend U.S. policy.

 

In closed-door peace talks, Trump’s envoy Jared Kushner has discussed a surprising bargain: Ukraine would cede territory to Russia in exchange for NATO membership. Moscow has fought for years to prevent Kyiv from joining the alliance, and Trump himself ruled it out early last year as unacceptable to Russia. Kushner and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff have raised the idea in discussions with European officials, though it’s unclear how seriously U.S. mediators are considering it. Bojan Pancevski reports on Washington’s latest efforts to break the stalemate in peace talks.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

The forces shaping the ‘new normal’ for war-era oil prices.

 
 
 

Oil prices have retreated from their recent highs, but they’re still nowhere near prewar levels. Persistent attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, soaring shipping costs and depleted global inventories are keeping prices elevated, even as oil production and exports recover. We charted the forces pushing and pulling oil prices to explain why $85 to $95 a barrel could be the market’s new reality for months or years to come.

8. THE NUMBER

 
−0.3%
 

The median profit margin on a home flip in San Antonio in the second quarter, making it the least-profitable major U.S. metro for house flippers. That figure doesn’t even account for renovation costs, property taxes or mortgage payments. Rising mortgage rates, skyrocketing property taxes and an oversupply of newly built homes have made flipping houses increasingly difficult. Three other Texas metros—Dallas, Austin and Houston—also rank among the five least-profitable major markets for house flippers.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

The U.S. Navy’s most sought-after snack is Uncrustables.

 

Fighter pilots won’t go on missions without them. Supply officers can’t stop thinking about them. And sailors suspect their peers of hoarding them. Aboard the USS George Washington in the Arabian Sea, the 5,000-person crew goes through 48,000 Uncrustables a month, and that’s still not enough to meet demand. The crustless PB&J sandwiches are so coveted that sailors sometimes trade them for other valuable items. One fighter pilot said he was more anxious about forgetting his Uncrustable than getting shot down by Iran.
